_about: Patch file of per-option rationales. Merged on top of the built-in glossary, which still fills any option left out here, so an entry only needs the lines the glossary cannot supply. Keyed options start with 'Correct'. Loaded by build.mjs and enforced there.

61.k: Cloud architecture is cheap to change, so the best practice is to automate and experiment rather than to get it right once up front.

r.A: The opposite of the cloud model. Redeploying is cheap here, so heavy up-front design is wasted effort.
r.B: Reservations mean a 1 or 3 year commitment. Test environments come and go, so On-Demand or Spot fits them.
r.C: Correct. Automation makes an experiment cost minutes, which is what lets architecture evolve instead of being frozen.
r.D: That is over-provisioning for a peak. Auto Scaling handles spikes without paying for idle capacity.

70.k: ElastiCache is a managed in-memory cache — Redis or Memcached — that sits in front of a database to absorb repeated reads.

r.A: Correct. Caching hot data in memory is exactly what ElastiCache is for, and read-heavy apps benefit most.
r.B: ElastiCache speaks Redis and Memcached. Ehcache is a Java library and is not one of its engines.
r.C: That describes AWS Marketplace, where you buy and launch third-party software.
r.D: DNS in the cloud is Amazon Route 53.

74.k: The AWS design principles are about automating change and removing anything that can fail alone — not about picking global services or fixing prices.

r.A: Region choice is driven by latency, cost and compliance. Neither global nor regional is automatically right.
r.B: Pay-as-you-go is a pricing model, not a design principle, and committing can be the cheaper choice.
r.C: Treating servers as fixed is the on-premises habit the cloud replaces — treat them as disposable instead.
r.D: Correct. Automation is what makes deployments repeatable and experiments cheap.
r.E: Correct. Removing single points of failure is the core of designing for failure.

103.k: Committing to 1 or 3 years in exchange for a lower rate is the Reserved Instance model, which AWS markets as 'save when you reserve'.

r.A: AWS does lower prices over time, but that is not a payment model you opt into.
r.B: Pay as you go is On-Demand — no commitment and no discount.
r.C: Pay less by using more is volume tiering, as in S3 storage pricing.
r.D: Correct. A 1 or 3 year commitment for a lower rate is the Reserved Instance model.

114.k: Glacier is archival storage: cheap to keep, slow to retrieve. It suits data you must keep but rarely read.

r.A: Correct. Active archives are read occasionally and kept for years, which is Glacier's exact use case.
r.B: Website assets must load in milliseconds. Serve them from S3 Standard, ideally behind CloudFront.
r.C: Correct. Long-term analytic data is queried infrequently and retained for compliance or trend analysis.
r.D: A live database needs millisecond access. Glacier retrievals take minutes to hours.
r.E: Cached data is by definition hot. That belongs in ElastiCache or CloudFront.

129.k: A TCO comparison counts the costs that differ between running on-premises and running on AWS — mostly the data-centre costs you stop paying.

r.A: You write the same application either way, so development cost does not change with the hosting decision.
r.B: Market research has nothing to do with where the workload runs.
r.C: Business analysis is a project cost, unaffected by the hosting model.
r.D: Correct. Servers, racks, power, cooling and space are exactly what disappears from the bill when you migrate.

134.k: Agility means the time between deciding you need a resource and having it drops from weeks to minutes.

r.A: Deploying in many Regions is global reach, a different advantage.
r.B: AWS does not sell customisable hardware — that is closer to what you give up when you leave the data centre.
r.C: Correct. Resources in minutes is the definition of agility, and it is what makes experimenting cheap.
r.D: Paying upfront for a discount is a pricing option, not agility.

150.k: Media destruction is part of the physical security AWS owns outright — a decommissioned device never leaves with data on it.

r.A: AWS never resells storage media. It is destroyed before it could leave the facility.
r.B: Correct. AWS follows NIST 800-88 style techniques and destroys media that cannot be securely wiped.
r.C: Remanufacturing would mean the device leaves AWS's control while it may still hold data.
r.D: Storing a dead device indefinitely is not a disposal process, and it leaves the data in existence.

161.k: A managed service trades control for speed: AWS runs the undifferentiated parts, so your team spends its time on the application.

r.A: Complete control is what you keep with EC2. Managed services deliberately take that control away.
r.B: Correct. Not having to build and operate the platform is what shortens time to launch.
r.C: Correct. Patching, backups and failover move to AWS, which is a direct drop in operational load.
r.D: Encryption is still the customer's decision on a managed service. Nothing removes that responsibility.
r.E: Managed services take patching away from developers rather than handing it to them.

165.k: Everything in AWS is an API call, so the point of the API is automation — the console, CLI and SDKs all sit on top of it.

r.A: Calling a resource through the API does not make the resource itself faster.
r.B: Provisioning speed comes from the cloud model. Clicking in the console is just as fast for one resource.
r.C: Automation changes what developers spend time on, but it is not a headcount argument.
r.D: Correct. Programmatic management is what makes scripting, infrastructure as code and CI/CD possible.

169.k: Service Catalog is a governance tool: IT publishes an approved list of products, and users may launch only those.

r.A: Descriptions and use cases live in the AWS documentation and the service pages.
r.B: Browsing AWS services is what the console and the product pages are for.
r.C: Correct. Publishing an approved, governed set of products for users to launch is exactly its purpose.
r.D: Defining infrastructure in a programming language is the AWS CDK.

177.k: AWS defines three control types: inherited, shared, and customer-specific. Shared controls apply to both layers, each side in its own context.

r.A: Controls that are solely the customer's are customer-specific controls, not shared ones.
r.B: Controls a customer inherits wholly from AWS are inherited controls — the physical and environmental ones.
r.C: Correct. AWS's wording is that shared controls apply to both the infrastructure layer and customer layers.
r.D: AWS is explicit that the two sides act in separate contexts rather than collaborating on the same control.

179.k: On EC2 the customer owns everything from the guest operating system upward, including their data and any software they install.

r.A: Correct. Your data is always yours to classify, encrypt and control, on every AWS service.
r.B: The underlying infrastructure — host, hypervisor, network fabric — is patched by AWS.
r.C: Managed databases are set up and operated by AWS. That is what makes them managed.
r.D: Hardware is AWS's, and customers never touch it.
r.E: Correct. Anything you install on the instance is yours to configure, license and patch.

180.k: The reasons to move are economic and operational — capacity that follows demand, and no data centre to fund.

r.A: Commercial licences still cost money on AWS. Some are bundled into the hourly rate, but nothing is free.
r.B: Only Basic support is free, and it does not include technical help.
r.C: Correct. Capacity that grows and shrinks with demand is something a fixed data centre cannot offer.
r.D: Customers cannot visit AWS data centres. Auditing is done through AWS Artifact reports instead.
r.E: Correct. Paying for what you use, with no idle hardware, is the headline financial argument.

189.k: DynamoDB is serverless NoSQL: no instances to size, no schema to define, and latency that stays flat as the table grows.

r.A: Correct. Throughput scales without you provisioning anything, which is the point of a serverless database.
r.B: Choosing instance sizes is RDS and EC2. DynamoDB has no instances to resize.
r.C: DynamoDB is NoSQL only. Relational workloads belong on RDS or Aurora.
r.D: Correct. Single-digit millisecond response at any scale is DynamoDB's headline characteristic.
r.E: DynamoDB is its own engine. MongoDB compatibility is DocumentDB; CouchDB is not offered at all.

204.k: Per-second billing with a 60-second minimum applies to Amazon Linux and Ubuntu. Other distributions still bill by the hour, rounded up.

r.A: Rounding the Amazon Linux instance up to whole hours ignores per-second billing.
r.B: Billing CentOS by the second is the trap. Per-second billing does not cover it.
r.C: Correct. Amazon Linux bills to the second; the CentOS instance rounds up from 4h23m to 5 hours.
r.D: This has both halves backwards.

227.k: Cloud Directory stores hierarchical data with more than one hierarchy over the same objects — org charts, device registries, course catalogues.

r.A: Correct. Multiple hierarchies over one set of objects is exactly what Cloud Directory was built for.
r.B: Real-time stream analysis is Kinesis.
r.C: Signing in with existing Active Directory credentials is AWS Directory Service.
r.D: Domain registration and DNS are Amazon Route 53.

228.k: Business Support answers a production system down case within one hour; the 15-minute target belongs to Enterprise for business-critical outages.

r.A: 12 hours is the Developer plan's target for a system impaired case, not a production outage.
r.B: 15 minutes applies to a business-critical system down case on Enterprise Support.
r.C: 24 hours is the general guidance target, the lowest urgency there is.
r.D: Correct. One hour is the published target for production system down on Business Support and above.

278.k: Economies of scale means AWS's aggregated purchasing across millions of customers lowers unit costs, and AWS passes those savings on.

r.A: Saving more as you consume more is volume tiering, a different pricing idea.
r.B: Prices have fallen repeatedly over the years, not risen with time.
r.C: Correct. Scale lowers AWS's unit costs, which is why it has cut prices many times.
r.D: Pay as you go is the On-Demand model, unrelated to scale.

286.k: Penetration testing means deliberately attacking your own systems to find exploitable weaknesses before someone else does.

r.A: Measuring response time from different locations is performance or latency testing.
r.B: Correct. Probing your own environment for weaknesses an attacker could use is what penetration testing is.
r.C: Checking which instances are unhealthy is what load balancer and Route 53 health checks do.
r.D: Finding bugs and errors is functional testing, which has nothing to do with security posture.

287.k: EMR runs managed big data frameworks — Spark, Hadoop, Hive, Presto — over large data sets on a cluster you can scale.

r.A: Cheap bulk backup is S3 and Glacier, not a compute cluster.
r.B: Exabyte-scale physical transfer is Snowmobile.
r.C: Correct. Processing very large data sets quickly is what a managed cluster is for.
r.D: Correct. Running and scaling Spark and Hadoop without building the cluster yourself is EMR's core job.
r.E: Docker orchestration is ECS, EKS or Fargate.

291.k: On RDS, AWS handles installation, patching, backups and failover. The customer keeps everything about access and network protection.

r.A: Correct. AWS installs and configures the database engine — you never touch the underlying software.
r.B: Protecting network traffic to the database, including TLS and security groups, remains yours.
r.C: Correct. The operating system underneath RDS is invisible to you and maintained by AWS.
r.D: Who may connect and with which credentials is always the customer's decision.
r.E: Security group rules are configured by the customer, on every service.

294.k: Storage Gateway is the hybrid bridge: on-premises applications see local storage while the data actually lives in AWS.

r.A: Building and running ETL jobs is AWS Glue.
r.B: Physical devices for shipping data are the Snow family.
r.C: Correct. Giving on-premises systems low-latency access to cloud storage is exactly what the gateway does.
r.D: Hardware-based key storage for compliance is AWS CloudHSM.

298.k: Route 53 does two things in exam questions: it is your DNS, and its routing policies steer traffic globally.

r.A: Point-to-point connectivity to a data centre is Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN.
r.B: Detecting configuration change is AWS Config.
r.C: Correct. Route 53 is a managed DNS service, including domain registration.
r.D: Correct. Latency, weighted, failover and geolocation policies are how it steers global traffic.
r.E: Infrastructure optimisation recommendations come from Trusted Advisor.

307.k: Reserved Instances come in two types: Standard for the deepest discount, and Convertible when you may need to change family.

r.A: Correct. Convertible RIs can be exchanged for a different family or OS during the term.
r.B: Expedited is a Glacier retrieval tier, not an RI type.
r.C: There is no bulk RI. Volume tiering is a separate pricing idea.
r.D: Spot is its own purchase option with no commitment, not a class of Reserved Instance.
r.E: Correct. Standard RIs give the largest discount but lock you to an instance family.

318.k: RDS supports six engines: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and Aurora. Anything else on the list is the answer to a 'not supported' question.

r.A: PostgreSQL is one of the six supported engines.
r.B: Oracle is supported, including bring-your-own-licence.
r.C: SQL Server is supported across several editions.
r.D: Correct. Teradata is a data warehouse product and is not an RDS engine.

338.k: DynamoDB is serverless, so capacity and scaling sit on AWS's side of the shared responsibility line.

r.A: A security team configures access controls; it does not add capacity to a managed service.
r.B: Developers design the table and its keys, but the scaling itself is not theirs to run.
r.C: Correct. Scaling the underlying capacity of a managed serverless database is AWS's job.
r.D: There is no infrastructure exposed for a DevOps team to scale.

390.k: S3 has no capacity to provision and no account-level ceiling. The only hard limit is 5 TB per individual object.

r.A: There is no 100 PB cap. The figure is invented.
r.B: Correct. Total storage is effectively unlimited; you simply pay for what you keep.
r.C: 5 TB is the maximum size of a single object, not of the account.
r.D: No exabyte ceiling exists either.

396.k: Two Availability Zones is the minimum that survives the loss of one. A single AZ is a single point of failure.

r.A: One AZ means one failure domain, which is the definition of not being highly available.
r.B: Correct. Two AZs is the smallest deployment that keeps running when one fails.
r.C: Three adds more headroom and is common for quorum systems, but it is not the minimum.
r.D: Four or more is beyond what the question asks and beyond what most Regions offer.

419.k: The benefit of the cloud is that the undifferentiated work goes away, freeing the team for work that makes money.

r.A: Permissive security is a risk, never a benefit, and AWS advises least privilege instead.
r.B: Correct. Handing racking, patching and capacity planning to AWS is what frees the team.
r.C: You do not control cloud network hardware — that is something you give up.
r.D: Choosing hardware vendors is an on-premises activity that the cloud removes.

469.k: Convertible RIs trade a little discount for the right to exchange into a different configuration of equal or greater value.

r.A: Dedicated RIs are about hardware tenancy, not about changing attributes.
r.B: Scheduled RIs reserve capacity in recurring time windows and are no longer offered for new purchases.
r.C: Correct. Exchange for equal or greater value is the defining feature of a Convertible RI.
r.D: Standard RIs can be sold on the marketplace but cannot be exchanged for a different family.

471.k: Spot capacity can be reclaimed with two minutes' notice, so it fits anything that can be interrupted and restarted.

r.A: Correct. Non-production work can absorb an interruption without anyone being affected.
r.B: Stateful work loses its state when the instance is reclaimed unless you engineer around it.
r.C: Applications that cannot be interrupted are the exact case Spot rules out.
r.D: Correct. Fault-tolerant and time-flexible is precisely the profile Spot was designed for.
r.E: A sensitive database needs to stay up, which Spot cannot promise.

477.k: Provisioning is fast because it is an API call away — no purchase order, no delivery, no racking.

r.A: A ticketing platform is the slow process the cloud replaces.
r.B: Code validation has nothing to do with how quickly infrastructure appears.
r.C: Correct. Resources already exist in AWS's fleet and are allocated to you programmatically in minutes.
r.D: AWS does not automate your vendor purchasing; it removes the need for it.

479.k: S3 is object storage: keys and objects in buckets, eleven nines of durability, reached over HTTP rather than mounted.

r.A: There is no global file system. S3 buckets live in a Region.
r.B: Correct. Objects addressed by key inside buckets is what object storage means.
r.C: A local file store attached to an instance is instance store or EBS.
r.D: A mountable network file system is Amazon EFS.
r.E: Correct. S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% durability.

538.k: Edge locations are caches. They bring copies of content near users and take repeat requests off the origin.

r.A: Applications run in Regions. Only Lambda@Edge runs limited code at the edge.
r.B: Correct. Serving from a nearby edge instead of the origin Region is the whole point.
r.C: NoSQL caching is DynamoDB Accelerator, which runs in a Region.
r.D: Correct. A cache hit never reaches the origin, so origin load drops.
r.E: Sending notifications is Amazon SNS.

541.k: Moving to AWS removes the data-centre work, so the business spends its effort on what the business actually does.

r.A: The bill changes shape from capital to operating expense; it does not disappear.
r.B: Putting a server in each customer's data centre is the opposite of centralising in the cloud.
r.C: Correct. Handing infrastructure operations to AWS is what frees the business to focus on its own work.
r.D: Guest operating systems still need patching. The responsibility stays with the customer.

552.k: On-Demand charges only for the time an instance actually runs, with no commitment and no upfront payment.

r.A: Bidding on price is Spot.
r.B: There is no daily rate — billing is per second or per hour depending on the OS.
r.C: Correct. Paying only for the time used, with nothing owed when the instance is stopped, is the On-Demand model.
r.D: Pre-paying for a lower rate describes Reserved Instances.

556.k: The cloud's value proposition is that you can start and stop at will — no contract, no purchase cycle, no idle hardware.

r.A: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud. Security IN the cloud is the customer's.
r.B: Correct. On-Demand requires no long-term contract, which is what makes trying things cheap.
r.C: Servers arrive in minutes, not days — that is the point.
r.D: AWS never manages your application code.

576.k: The cloud lowers both halves: no upfront hardware purchase, and a lower per-unit running cost thanks to AWS's scale.

r.A: Both being greater would mean the cloud is simply more expensive, which is not the argument.
r.B: Usage costs vary with what you run; they are not fixed.
r.C: There is no large upfront cost to speak of, which is the main financial draw.
r.D: Correct. Lower upfront investment and lower variable cost together are the standard TCO claim.

738.k: Spot suits work whose start time is negotiable, because AWS can take the capacity back at two minutes' notice.

r.A: Correct. Flexibility about when the job runs is what lets you absorb an interruption.
r.B: Mission-critical means it must not stop, which rules Spot out.
r.C: Dedicated capacity is Capacity Reservations or Dedicated Hosts.
r.D: If an instance must not be stopped, Spot is the wrong purchase option by definition.

740.k: Lambda bills on two dimensions only: the number of requests, and duration multiplied by the memory you allocated.

r.A: Bidding on an hourly price is Spot.
r.B: Upfront terms are Reserved Instances and Savings Plans, and there is no 5-year term.
r.C: Lambda charges nothing for permanent storage — that would be S3, EFS or a database bill.
r.D: Correct. Requests plus compute time, measured in GB-seconds, is the whole Lambda price.

755.k: Security IN the cloud is the customer's: your data, your encryption choices, and the network rules around your resources.

r.A: Virtualisation is AWS's layer. Customers have no access to the hypervisor.
r.B: Hardware is AWS's responsibility in every case.
r.C: Correct. Whether and how to encrypt your data is always your decision.
r.D: Facilities — buildings, power, cooling — are wholly AWS's.
r.E: Correct. Security groups and network ACLs are configured by the customer.

770.k: Because capacity can be added and removed on demand, you never have to predict how much hardware to buy.

r.A: Correct. Stop guessing capacity is one of the six advantages, and it is what elasticity buys you.
r.B: Existing hardware contracts are what you are moving away from.
r.C: Costs move with usage. Fixing them regardless of traffic is the on-premises model.
r.D: AWS Artifact helps with audits — it does not let you avoid them.

801.k: The advantage is elasticity: capacity follows demand, so no one has to forecast a peak years ahead.

r.A: AWS does not inspect customer data. Ownership and access stay with you.
r.B: Nothing is secure by default. Encryption and access control are choices you make.
r.C: Correct. Capacity that scales on demand removes the guesswork from planning.
r.D: AWS supplies evidence through Artifact, but your compliance remains yours to manage.

807.k: High availability means the application keeps answering when an individual component or Availability Zone fails.

r.A: Round-the-clock support is a Support plan feature, not an architectural property.
r.B: Correct. Staying accessible through a component failure is the definition of high availability.
r.C: Paying on demand is a pricing model.
r.D: Deploying worldwide is global reach; it improves latency, not necessarily availability.

814.k: Amazon Linux bills per second with a 60-second minimum, so the customer pays for the exact runtime.

r.A: Dropping the seconds would be per-minute billing, which AWS does not use.
r.B: Correct. Per-second billing applies to Amazon Linux, so the exact 3h5m6s is charged.
r.C: Rounding up to the next minute is not how the meter works.
r.D: Rounding to whole hours applies to Windows and some commercial Linux distributions, not Amazon Linux.

851.k: Infrastructure as code means the environment is defined in a template that can be versioned, reviewed and re-run.

r.A: Moving physical hardware into AWS data centres is not something customers do at all.
r.B: Third-party audits are unrelated to how you define infrastructure.
r.C: You never hand application code to AWS to run on your behalf.
r.D: Correct. Templates provision the environment repeatably, which is the whole idea.

854.k: CloudFormation takes a JSON or YAML template and creates, updates and deletes the described resources as one stack.

r.A: Correct. Modelling resources in a template and provisioning them from it is what CloudFormation does.
r.B: Updating application code is CodeDeploy and the rest of the developer tools.
r.C: Setting up a data lake is AWS Lake Formation.
r.D: Billing reports come from Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report.

868.k: The model is called shared for a reason: AWS secures the cloud, the customer secures what they put in it.

r.A: The customer owns their half, but not the facilities, hardware or hypervisor.
r.B: AWS owns its half, but never your data, your IAM policies or your security groups.
r.C: Correct. Both parties hold responsibilities, and where the line falls depends on the service.
r.D: Governing bodies define standards. They hold no responsibility for your environment.

876.k: Hybrid means part of the workload runs in AWS and part stays on-premises, joined by Direct Connect, VPN, Outposts or Storage Gateway.

r.A: Everything on-premises is the traditional model, not hybrid.
r.B: A colocation centre is still someone else's data centre, not the AWS Cloud.
r.C: Everything in AWS is the cloud deployment model.
r.D: Correct. A foot in both places is exactly what hybrid means.

901.k: The cloud replaces a large capital purchase made in advance with a smaller variable charge for what you actually consume.

r.A: This states the trade backwards — variable costs are what you move to, not away from.
r.B: Correct. Capital investment becomes variable spend, which is why the upfront cost falls.
r.C: Provisioning for peak is the over-buying habit the cloud removes.
r.D: Fixed scale is the opposite of what elasticity offers.

937.k: The cloud's value proposition is that you can start and stop at will — no contract, no purchase cycle, no idle hardware.

r.A: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud. Security IN the cloud is the customer's.
r.B: Correct. On-Demand requires no long-term contract, which is what makes trying things cheap.
r.C: Servers arrive in minutes, not days — that is the point.
r.D: AWS never manages your application code.

939.k: The customer owns the application and everything above the operating system. AWS owns the hardware, hypervisor and facilities.

r.A: Physical hardware is AWS's, and customers never touch it.
r.B: The hypervisor is part of the infrastructure AWS maintains.
r.C: Nobody from the customer visits an AWS data centre, so there is no access list to provide.
r.D: Correct. Your application and its updates are always yours to manage.

971.k: Elasticity means capacity is added when demand rises and released when it falls, so performance holds without over-buying.

r.A: Spreading traffic across Regions is Route 53 or Global Accelerator, not elasticity.
r.B: Archiving logs to cut storage cost is an S3 lifecycle policy.
r.C: AWS never picks services for you.
r.D: Correct. Adjusting capacity to match demand, in both directions, is exactly what elasticity is.

975.k: The Simple Monthly Calculator priced a described architecture before you built it. It has since been replaced by the Pricing Calculator.

r.A: Comparing on-premises with colocation is what a TCO analysis does, not a monthly estimate.
r.B: Correct. It estimates the monthly bill from the resources you say you plan to run.
